title: Buddha-nature views
hookLine: some schools teach inborn Buddha-nature; others speak of what can be developed

cards: A monk comes to the old Chinese teacher Zhaozhou, whom you met over tea in year three, with what sounds like an easy question. The sutras say every living being has Buddha-nature. So does a dog have Buddha-nature?
Zhaozhou answers with one syllable. Wu. No.
Nothing. Zen students still sit with that single word, turning it over until something gives. Why would a teacher who knew the sutras say no?

teach.b: First, the inborn view. A group of Mahayana scriptures, among them the Mahaparinirvana Sutra, teach that all beings have Buddha-nature, sometimes called the tathagatagarbha, the womb or seed of a Buddha.

Awakening isn't built from scratch. It's already there, covered over like gold in the earth or a jewel sewn into a beggar's coat, and practice uncovers it. Zen and other schools of East Asia grew up with this teaching.
Second, the koan. So why does Zhaozhou say no?

teach.h: WU: A GATE, NOT A DOCTRINE.
teach.b: Zen teachers say Wu isn't a doctrine to agree or disagree with. It's a gate. Holding Buddha-nature as an idea can become one more thing to cling to, and Wu cuts the rope.
The Theravada speaks less of a hidden Buddha inside and more of qualities to be grown: generosity, ethics, patience, wisdom, the perfections cultivated over a long path.
The Pali texts do have a striking line: the Anguttara Nikaya says the mind is luminous, stained by defilements that arrive from outside.
Some teachers take that as a seed of the inborn view; others read it simply as a reason to practice. Fourth, voices within one tradition.
Tibetan schools debate this too. Some say Buddha-nature is the mind's emptiness, which makes growth possible; others, a radiant nature with qualities already complete. Each explains itself carefully.
And some teachers say a practitioner needs both: trust that it's there, and effort to grow it.

how: In Zen, students may work with the koan of Zhaozhou's dog for a long time with a teacher; Theravada practitioners speak of cultivating the perfections, and Tibetan monastic colleges study and debate the nature of Buddha-nature.

o: whether a Buddha can be born into any family or caste
whether animals can be reborn as humans in a later life
whether awakening is already in us or grown through practice

games.q: born or grown: tap the pairs.
p: the seed of a Buddha in every being

s: Zhaozhou's Wu means Zen rejects Buddha-nature
Zen teachers say the word is a gate, not a doctrine, cutting the rope of clinging to an idea.
the Anguttara Nikaya calls the mind luminous
and says it is stained by defilements that arrive from outside.
all Tibetan schools explain Buddha-nature the same way
some call it the mind's emptiness, others a radiant nature with qualities complete.

games.q: you're Zhaozhou. a monk asks: the sutras say every being has Buddha-nature. does a dog? what do you answer?
o: yes, of course; the sutras say so.
games.why: Zhaozhou says Wu. Zen teachers say it isn't a denial of the sutras but a gate to sit with until something gives.

practice: For the first minute, rest as if there's nothing to add, as if the clear, kind mind is already here under the noise, like sky behind clouds.
For the second, choose one quality to grow, patience perhaps, or generosity, and breathe as if you're watering a seed. There's no need to decide which minute was right.

wordCard.voice: Buddha-nature views. Some schools teach that awakening is already present in every being, waiting to be uncovered; others speak of qualities grown on the path. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit tathagatagarbha: the womb or seed of the Buddha, one name for Buddha-nature.

carryVoice: Your line: born or grown. A seed to trust, and a seed to water. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahaparinirvana Sutra (Mahayana), on Buddha-nature in all beings
